cues: This is the HollowVale Harbor Historical Society. This broadcast is recorded for the record. Please do not adjust your set.
Tonight: the complete history of HollowVale Harbor, from the first boat to the last.
In the spring of 1803, three whaling ships came around Gull Point in a fog so thick the sailors tied ropes between their wrists.
They found a deep, quiet harbor, ringed with black rock, and water so still it held the sky like a mirror.
Captain Elias Vane wrote in his log: the fog here is kinder than the sea. We will stay.
By winter there were eleven houses, a smokehouse, and a church with no bell. The bell, they said, would come later.
In 1871, the town built a lighthouse on Gull Point. Sixty feet tall, painted white, with a lamp that could be seen nine miles out to sea.
Its first keeper was a quiet man named Abel Morrow. He kept a careful log, and nearly every entry ends the same way. Light lit. Fog thick. All quiet.
Until the autumn of 1874, when the entries begin to change.
October the third. Something knocked at the lamp room door. No one was there.
October the ninth. The knocking again. Three times. It came from the fog side of the glass.
October the fourteenth. I did not answer it. I will not answer it.
Abel Morrow kept the light for thirty more years. He never once answered the knocking.
Part three. The keeper who answered.
In 1904, a new keeper arrived. A young man from the city, who did not believe in old men's logs.
On his first foggy night, he heard the knocking. He took his lantern, and he went down to answer it.
In the morning, his lantern was found on the rocks below the light. Still burning. The keeper was never found.
On the morning of June the eleventh, 1923, thirty one fishing boats left the harbor in clear weather.
By noon, a fog came in off the water faster than anyone had ever seen.
None of the boats came back. No wreckage was ever found.
But for seven nights afterward, the people of HollowVale heard the boats' bells ringing out in the fog. One for each boat. Thirty one bells.
On the eighth night, the bells stopped. And the church, at last, had a bell of its own. No one in town would say where it came from.
WKRS went on the air in 1948, from a small booth above the harbor. It played music, read the marine weather, and kept the town company through the long foggy nights.
Its most beloved voice was Ruth Calloway, host of Night Owl, from midnight to six.
People said that when Ruth was on the air, the fog stayed politely out at sea.
In the autumn of 2015, at 3:12 in the morning, the WKRS transmitter began to sing by itself. No one was touching the controls.
Every radio in HollowVale Harbor turned itself on.
The fog came up the streets, house by house, and the porch lights went on one by one, as if someone were walking from door to door.
By sunrise, the harbor was empty. Four hundred people. Every boat still tied at the dock. Every kettle still warm.
Ruth Calloway was never found. The few who were left call that night the Hollowtide. And some nights, between the stations, you can still hear her.
That concludes the history of HollowVale Harbor.
The Historical Society reminds you. If you hear a bell in the fog, do not go down to the water. And if something knocks, do not answer it.
